$comment: Transcribed from place-name-shapes-reference.md (part 1). Data only: no plugin logic. Source elements and examples are kept for reference and never output.

categories.label: Personal name
categories.covers: A named individual, usually an owner or founder

categories.label: Ethnic or cultural group
categories.covers: A people distinct from the namers

categories.label: Supernatural being
categories.covers: Demons, dragons, goblins and similar beings

categories.label: Landform
categories.covers: A nearby hill, slope or spur

categories.label: Built feature
categories.covers: A road, mill, fort or other structure

categories.label: Earlier or district name
categories.covers: An older place name or a territory name used as the specific

categories.label: Colour
categories.covers: Colour of water, soil or vegetation

categories.label: Position or direction
categories.covers: Compass point, upper or lower, middle

categories.label: Empty slot
categories.covers: No specific; the generic stands alone

generics.sense: Early sense: an enclosure with dwelling
Later sense: an administrative or lordly unit
Very early English settlement, often near Roman roads

sourceElements: OE worþ, worþig (South West), worþign (West Midlands)

examples.common: Edgbaston, Kettleby; Norton, Westby; Newton; Hilton; Marston, Fordham; Ashton, Ashby; Stratton, Chesterton; Kingston, Charlton; Luton, Tamworth; Barton
examples.occasional: Shipton, Swinton; Denby, Ingleby; Clayton, Stanton; Kirkby; Mickleton; Langton; Brampton; Somerton; Birmingham

overrides.note: Folk-group territory (-ingas): takes only personal name (Hastings, Reading).

examples.common: Hastings, Reading

overrides.note: Village where Norse (bý): personal name and ethnic or cultural group are both strongly Common (Grimsby, Normanby, Irby).
Home farm of an estate (mains): takes earlier or district name (Mains of X).

generics.sense: Daughter settlement of a larger one
Often a special-purpose or outlying site
Often dairy or another single product
Farm worked for a religious house
Medieval lordly or forest stock farm
Smallholders dependent on a larger farm
English settlement beside a Roman vicus

examples.common: Scunthorpe; Northwich, Middlewich; Butterwick, Chiswick; Gatwick
examples.occasional: Newthorpe; Basingstoke; Tavistock; Bishopstoke; Woodthorpe; Greenwich; Berwick

overrides.note: Dependent or secondary settlement (þorp): dominated by personal name.
Specialised farm (wīc): produce and domestic animal are its strongest pairings.
Outlying place (stoc): Empty slot is Common, usually with a later affix (Stoke Mandeville, Stoke-on-Trent).
Monastic outlying farm (grange): usually takes the owning house; treat as status or role. Regional: status or role keeps its group tier.

generics.sense: Lived-in place, often a single holding
Site of a house and its yard

generics.meaning: Small enclosed field by a house

examples.common: Didcot, Lowestoft; Northcote, Westcott; Caldecote; Newbold, Newbottle
examples.occasional: Walcot; Langtoft; Woodhall; Colerne; Ryecroft

overrides.note: Cottage (cot): unusually strong pull towards quality or condition (“cold cottages”: Caldecote, Calcot).
Dwelling (W bod): same pattern, generic-first (Bodedern).

groups.label: Seasonal and upland settlement

examples.common: Hawkshead, Anglezarke, Grimsargh; Hafod Uchaf
examples.occasional: Seascale; Portinscale

notes: Season is Unlikely because it is redundant.

generics.sense: Dug source of clay, stone or chalk

examples.common: Northwich, Westmill; Putney; Newport; Chelsea; Lambeth, Rotherhithe
examples.occasional: Maidenhead; Erith; Droitwich; Langport; Whitehaven; Bridport

overrides.note: Landing place (hȳþ): named after what came ashore, so produce and domestic animal are especially strong.
Market (cēping): mostly survives as an affix rather than a generic (see §7). Kept as a generic with the group profile.

groups.label: Religious: Christian

generics.sense: Senior church serving a wide area
Consecrated enclosure named for a saint
Norse name for places of the papar

examples.common: Kilbride, Felixkirk, Padstow; Ormskirk, Kidderminster; Westminster, Upchurch; Axminster, Llandaff
examples.occasional: Whitchurch; Newchurch; Kilmore, Papa Stour; Bristol; Chepstow; Leominster

overrides.note: Saint’s church enclosure (llan, lan, cill): dominated by saint or holy person, generic-first.
British church community and Hermitage: Empty slot is Common (Eccles, Dysart).

notes: Deity + church is unattested but is an obvious lever for syncretic religions in fantasy settings.

groups.label: Religious: pre-Christian and sacred

generics.sense: Spring with sacred or healing status

examples.common: Harrow, Wye; Peper Harow, Snelland
examples.occasional: Holywell

overrides.note: Saint or holy person is Occasional for holy springs only.

notes: In real names, deity names attach more often to landscape generics (clearings, hill-spurs) than to shrine generics.

groups.label: Religious: burial and memorial

examples.common: Taplow, Hounslow, Bledlow
examples.occasional: Wodnesbeorg; Drakelow; Thingoe, Mutlow; Cairngorm; Ludlow; Beddgelert

notes: Burial mounds are the strongest real-world home of the spiritual and fantastical categories.

generics.sense: Fort, often but not always Roman
Defensive tower, especially in the Border

examples.common: Banbury, Bewcastle; Westbury, Sudbury; Aldbury, Newcastle; Doncaster, Lancaster, Exeter, Cardiff; Canterbury, Worcester; Gloucester, Winchester, Carlisle, Caernarfon
examples.occasional: Wednesbury, Wansdyke; Grim’s Ditch, Devil’s Dyke; Shrewsbury

overrides.note: Dyke, boundary earthwork (dīc): deity and supernatural being rise to Common (earthworks credited to gods, devils and giants).
Beacon: usually takes the hill’s own name; treat as earlier or district name. Regional: earlier or district name keeps its group tier.

generics.sense: Later sense of burh in the south

examples.common: Kingsbury, Abbotsbury
examples.occasional: Llyswen; Woodhall

examples.common: Tynwald, Dingwall, Thingwall, Spellow, Plaistow, Bath

generics.sense: Spring-fed, often on chalk; sometimes seasonal
Stream and the valley it runs in
Where a river meets sea or lake

examples.common: Blackburn, Redbourn; Sherborne, Fulbrook; Ashbourne; Winterbourne; Exmouth, Aberystwyth, Inverness
examples.occasional: Otterburn; Cranbrook; Rushbrooke; Bradbourne; Westbrook; Millbrook

overrides.note: River mouth, Confluence and Waterfall take river or stream name almost by default.

examples.common: Whitwell, Blackwell; Caldwell; Bakewell, Windermere; Ashwell, Haslemere; Cranwell; Grasmere
examples.occasional: Chalfont; Halliwell; Holywell; Buttermere; Loch Ness; Langmere

examples.common: Sedgemoor; Alrewas, Ellerker; Blackmore
examples.occasional: Chat Moss; Romney Marsh

examples.occasional: Foulness, Arncliffe; Durness; Rubha nan Gall; Caithness; Solway Firth, Moray Firth

groups.label: Crossings and routes

generics.sense: Neck of land where boats were dragged

overrides.note: River crossing (ford): the broadest profile in the inventory.

examples.common: Oxford, Shefford, Swinford; Ashford, Oakford; Stanford, Sandford, Chalford; Bradford, Langford; Fairford, Fulford; Ammanford; Bedford; Stratford, Milford
examples.occasional: Hertford; Cranford; Bramford; Blackford; Twyford

overrides.note: Bridge, causeway, ferry.

examples.common: Weybridge; Uxbridge; Trowbridge, Stockbridge

overrides.note: Paved or Roman road, way or track, lane.

examples.common: Watling Street, Ermine Street; Stane Street

overrides.note: Pass, gap or notch, swing gate.

examples.common: Bealach na Bà; Bwlch y Groes

overrides.note: Isthmus, portage.

examples.common: Tarbert

notes: Assumption: causeway, ferry, lane, gap and swing gate were assigned to these profiles by analogy and should be reviewed.

overrides.note: Woodland, then clearing (lēah): the strongest home of deity names in England. Regional: deity keeps its group tier.
Woodland swine pasture (denn): domestic animal is Unlikely (redundant).
